description: I'm passionate about space exploration, technology, and creative storytelling. I want to bring NASA's forgotten equipment on the Moon and Mars back to life through engaging stories. I'm looking for creative and dedicated teammates with skills in research, writing, design, coding, and presentation. Let's work together to make space history interesting and unforgettable!
summary:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive space story we built in PictoBlox. Players explore all eight planets, the Moon and deep space, guided by an astronaut called Astro. On each world they tap the robots NASA left behind, such as the Apollo 11 lander Eagle, the Opportunity rover, the Ingenuity helicopter, Cassini and Voyager 1. Each machine tells its own story in the first person, with narration and sound effects. It explains why it was sent, what it discovered and how its mission ended.

This answers the challenge by turning forgotten equipment into characters people can care about, instead of a list of mission facts. A short eight-question quiz checks what players learned and keeps score.

It matters because most students only hear about active missions. Stories like Opportunity’s, built to work for 90 days and lasting 14 years, show how good engineering leads to discovery and can inspire the next generation of explorers. The simple tap-and-listen design lets young learners use it without help.
details:
What it does and how it works
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive, narrated story game made in PictoBlox. The player starts at a menu with an astronaut guide, Astro, and can take a Solar System Tour, visit the Moon, go to Deep Space or take a quiz.

  • Planets: on the tour, the player taps any of the 8 planets. Each planet has its own scene, and Astro narrates its story with on-screen captions.
  • Robots: on each world the player taps a spacecraft or robot. Eleven of them speak in the first person, in their own voice. They include Eagle, the Lunar Rover, Opportunity, Ingenuity, Voyager 1 and 2, MESSENGER, Magellan, Skylab, Galileo and Cassini.
  • Quiz: an 8-question quiz covers all the planets, reads each question aloud and keeps score.

The project uses PictoBlox’s broadcast messages to switch scenes and a shared variable so only one voice speaks at a time.

Benefits and intended impact
The project turns dry mission data into stories that students remember. It teaches the history of NASA’s older missions, which are rarely taught, and shows how engineering leads to discovery. It needs no instructions, so young learners can use it alone, and the narration helps those who find reading difficult. We hope it inspires the next generation of explorers.

Tools and software

  • PictoBlox, which uses block coding, for all the game logic.
  • Python to generate the artwork as SVG images and to synthesize the sound effects, such as the launch, whoosh and quiz chimes.
  • The eSpeak NG text-to-speech engine for the narration voices.
  • FFmpeg to process the audio.
  • Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic, helped us write the scripts. Please check the challenge’s rules on AI use and mention this if required.

We used no extra hardware.

Creativity
The challenge asks for stories, so we let the machines tell their own, which gives each one a personality. Eagle’s lower half is still at Tranquility Base, and Ingenuity flew far beyond its plan. Each robot has its own voice, and the whole solar system is one connected journey.

What we considered

  • Accuracy: facts come from NASA sources, and we checked them against NASA’s Resources tab.
  • Age: short sentences and big buttons suit school-age players.
  • Accessibility: captions match the narration word for word.
  • Honesty: the artwork and voices are computer-generated, not real NASA images or recordings, and we credit NASA for the facts.
